Recording 4: Miking a Guitar Amp

Which mic, where on the speaker, how far, at what angle; a room mic, two mics and their phase; DI and re-amping.

A guitar amp’s sound is mostly its speaker: little above 5–6 kHz comes out of one at all, and what does changes a lot across its face. So the first decision is not which mic, but where to put it.

Which mic

  • Dynamic (the SM57 type): the usual first choice. Takes any level, sounds right close up, its lift around 4–6 kHz helps a guitar cut through. Cheap enough to own two.
  • Ribbon: darker and smoother; takes the fizz off a distorted amp. A figure-8, so its back hears the room (or the ceiling) as much as its front hears the speaker. Some ribbons can’t take a loud amp close up; check the manual, and never send them phantom power from a miswired cable (Recording 2).
  • Condenser (large diaphragm): detailed and open, best a little back from the amp, or as a room mic.
  • Two at once: a dynamic and a ribbon side by side on the same speaker, blended, is a classic.

Where on the speaker

Shine a torch through the grille cloth to find the speaker and its dust cap. In a cabinet with several speakers, listen to each with your ear close (at low volume) and pick the best-sounding one; they are rarely identical.

  • On the dust cap: brightest, most bite, can be harsh or fizzy.
  • At the cap’s edge: bright and full. Start here.
  • On the cone: warmer and rounder.
  • Near the edge: dark and woolly, rarely what you want.

A centimetre matters. Have someone move the mic while you listen in closed headphones in another room.

Distance and angle

  • Close (1–5 cm from the grille cloth): the speaker’s own sound, little room, and the most proximity bass. Most rock and pop guitar is recorded like this.
  • Further back (20–60 cm): the speaker’s sound “comes together”; the room starts to join in.
  • Angled 30–45°: a little darker, less fizz, without moving across the speaker. Try it before reaching for the EQ.

Drag the mic across the speaker, then change the distance, angle, mic and room:

A room mic, and two mics

A second mic 1–2 m back (a condenser, or a ribbon) records the amp in the room. Blend a little under the close mic for size. Two mics on one amp are two distances, so check their phase: flip the polarity of one and keep whichever sounds fuller, and keep two close mics the same distance from the speaker (Recording 3: Phase). An open-back combo can be miked from behind as well; the back mic faces the other way, so flip its polarity.

Volume

The amp doesn’t need to be loud to sound good on a mic. Many amps sound best with their power section working, but a small amp turned up often records better than a big one turned down. Loud amps go in another room, or facing a wall with a blanket over them and the mic, so they don’t bleed into everything else (Recording 3: Bleed).

DI and re-amping

Record a DI of the guitar (straight from the guitar through a DI box or the interface’s instrument input) at the same time as the mic. Later the clean DI can be sent back out to an amp (re-amping, through a re-amp box) or into an amp simulator, if the sound you chose doesn’t fit the mix. Bass is usually recorded with a DI and a mic on the cab, blended.
